edges.effect_quant: Open-label pediatric studies have reported behavioral improvement after microbiota transfer therapy, including a 2017 study in 18 children, a 2021 trial in 40 children with ASD plus GI symptoms, a 2022 repeated-WMT series with 42 enrolled children, and a 2025 prospective cohort in which 25 ASD participants received FMT and improved at 3 months.
edges.population: children with autism spectrum disorder, usually selected for concurrent gastrointestinal symptoms or constipation and treated in uncontrolled specialty-center protocols
edges.mechanism: Proposed benefit runs through the microbiome-gut-brain axis, with FMT potentially altering microbial metabolites, immune signaling, gut barrier function, bowel habits, and neurotransmitter-related pathways that may secondarily influence behavior.
edges.summary: Small uncontrolled pediatric studies repeatedly report improvements in autism rating scales after FMT or washed microbiota transplantation. The signal is intriguing but remains highly provisional, and it appears most plausible in selected children with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms rather than as a general autism treatment.
edges.caveats: There are no randomized controlled trials, most studies are open-label or retrospective, and many children received concurrent behavioral or medical therapies. Regression to the mean, caregiver expectancy, and selection of GI-symptomatic subgroups are major concerns, so this should be read as early subgroup-specific evidence rather than established efficacy.

evidence.notes: Microbiota Transfer Therapy alters gut ecosystem and improves gastrointestinal and autism symptoms: an open-label study.
